newsitem.title: SRI LANKA: Sri Lanka's growth forecasts revised up by EIU.
newsitem.headline: Sri Lanka's growth forecasts revised up by EIU.

text.p: COLOMBO, March 20 (Rueter) - The Economist Intelligence Unit (EIU) has revised upwards Sri Lanka's medium-term growth forecasts, but has said the country's budget deficit may be difficult to tame due to a continuing civil war.

"The EIU has this quarter revised upwards to 5.5 percent per year its forecast for average annual GDP (gross domestic product) growth during the 1997-2001 forecast period," it said in a report made available to Reuters on Thursday.
The previous forecast for the same period was 4.6 percent, it said.

Policy reforms outlined in the 1997 budget and recent moves to address pressing economic issues such as the high cost of finance and infrastructural inadequacy justify cautious optimism about Sri Lanka's medium-term economic prospects, the report said.

"More realistic budget targets, especially for revenue from privatisation, will facilitate a gradual reduction of the fiscal deficit, although the unpredictability of the civil war will remain a serious threat to fiscal stability," it says.

Sri Lanka's war with Liberation Tigers of Tamil Eelam rebels, who are fighting for a separate state in the north and east, has cost the country nearly five percent of gross domestic product (GDP) in recent years.

Although the government projects the budget deficit at 7.3 percent of GDP in 1997 and 5.2 percent in 1998, the EIU report pegged it at 7.5 percent of GDP in the early part of the forecast period, later falling to 5.6 percent.

The report said a more determined approach to rectify infrastructure deficiencies, particularly in power, telecommunications and industrial infrastructrure, also augur well for an improvement in the overall operating environment.
A power shortage due to failure of monsoon rains in 1996 had dragged GDP growth down to around four percent last year.
Manufacturing and agriculture, badly hit by the 1996 drought, are seen recovering, with manufacturing remaining the engine of growth, the report said.
The EIU is a division of The Economist Newspaper Ltd.
